{"id":"PKIX-55jb","title":"pkix-path never applies dNSName name constraints to the CN; OpenSSL does","description":"pkix-path accepts chains OpenSSL rejects as name-constraint violations, because it never consults the subject commonName. Both CN references in pkix-path/src/lib.rs are inside #[cfg(test)] modules; production code looks only at dNSName SANs.

Demonstrated, not inferred. Three chains, root -> ICA (nameConstraints) -> EE, built with openssl and run through both oracles via 'pkix-difftest single':

  CN                 EE SANs      ICA constraint              openssl                      pkix-path
  bar.example.com    none         excluded DNS:bar.example.com  Fail: excluded subtree viol.  Pass
  John Smith         email only   permitted DNS:example.com     OK                            -
  notallowed.test    email only   permitted DNS:example.com     Fail: permitted subtree viol. Pass

So OpenSSL's rule is: when a certificate presents no dNSName SAN, apply dNSName constraints to the commonName if the CN is hostname-shaped, in both the permitted and excluded directions. A CN that is not hostname-shaped ('John Smith') is skipped, so the check does not reject certificates whose CN was never a hostname. pkix-path passes all three.

Reproduce with:
  openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout root.key -out root.pem -subj /CN=Root -addext basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE -addext keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign
  # ICA ext: basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE / keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign / nameConstraints=critical,excluded;DNS:bar.example.com
  # EE  ext: basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE / keyUsage=critical,digitalSignature  (and NO subjectAltName)
  # EE subject: /CN=bar.example.com
  openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted ica.pem ee.pem

Why it matters beyond the abstract. RFC 5280 does not require checking the CN, and reading a CN as a hostname is deprecated (RFC 6125 §6.4.4), which pkix-identity::verify_dns_name honours -- it returns MissingSan rather than falling back. But RFC 7672 §3.2.3 still REQUIRES CN fallback for SMTP DANE, and pkix-dane::verify_smtp_name does it via verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback. That path is reachable only under TlsaUsage::DaneTa -- DANE-EE(3) returns NotRequired per §3.2.1 and PKIX-TA/PKIX-EE are refused as PkixUsageUnusable -- and DANE-TA does validate a chain, so an intermediate's dNSName constraints are in play.

Composed: an intermediate forbidden from bar.example.com issues an EE with no SAN and CN=bar.example.com; pkix-path finds no dNSName SAN so the exclusion matches nothing and the path is valid; verify_smtp_name then matches the CN and reports Matched. The CA's exclusion is evaded.

Note this needs no wildcard. It was found while chasing a wildcard-CN variant of PKIX-bhtl, and the wildcard turned out to be irrelevant: a CN equal to the excluded name evades the constraint by itself. PKIX-bhtl's fix does not cover this, because that one bounded a wildcard SAN's coverage and this certificate has no SAN at all.

Recommended fix: mirror OpenSSL. In check_name_constraints, when the certificate presents no dNSName SAN, also check a hostname-shaped commonName against the dNSName subtrees in both directions.

The decision to make is the hostname-shaped test, because it is a heuristic in a security boundary and it is what bounds the false-rejection tail. OpenSSL's answer is observable above: it skipped 'John Smith' and checked 'notallowed.test'. A reasonable rule is at least one dot plus all labels being LDH (letters, digits, hyphen) with no spaces, which admits both demonstrated cases correctly. Too loose and a descriptive CN gets read as a hostname and rejected; too tight and an attacker picks a CN that evades the test but is still matched by verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback, which has no such heuristic -- so the two tests must agree, the same coupling requirement PKIX-bhtl's fix had with pkix-identity's wildcard matcher.

Alternative considered and dispreferred: expose the accumulated constraints on ValidatedPath so the DANE layer can check a CN it actually matched. That has no false-rejection tail at all, since it only checks a name the certificate is genuinely asserting, but ValidatedPath exposes only anchor_index and depth today, so it needs new public API, and it leaves pkix-path accepting a chain OpenSSL rejects -- which is a divergence worth closing on its own, independent of DANE.

Also worth noting: INTEROP.md's 'Current status' says zero correctness regressions were detected against OpenSSL across the 247 classifiable PKITS chains. That remains true -- PKITS has no vector of this shape -- but this is a case where pkix-path is more lenient than OpenSSL, which is the opposite direction from every divergence currently documented there.","status":"open","priority":1,"issue_type":"bug","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-11-28T05:19:09.415463437Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-11-28T05:19:09.415463437Z"}

{"notes":"CORRECTION to this bead's own description: it overstated severity. I filed it P1 claiming the DANE composition was exploitable. It was not.

pkix-chain's SMTP DANE entry point already refused this entire shape, unconditionally, with SmtpDaneFailure::ConstrainedPathWithoutDnsId -- closed earlier under PKIX-skxt, with a fixture (pkix-chain/tests/fixtures/constrained-no-san/) and two tests whose comments set out the same composition analysis I had just redone. My reachability trace stopped at pkix-dane::verify_smtp_name and never looked at the umbrella crate above it, which is where the composition actually happens. I found this only because my pkix-path change made those two tests fail.

What remains true, and is why the fix is still worth having: pkix-path accepted a chain OpenSSL rejects, and pkix-path is published on its own, so a consumer validating a path without going through pkix-chain got the lenient answer. The divergence was real; the live-bypass framing was wrong.

FIXED. pkix-path now reads a host-name-shaped commonName as a dNSName identity when the certificate presents no dNSName SAN, and bounds it against the subtrees in both directions, matching OpenSSL on all three demonstrated chains:

  CN                 EE SANs      ICA constraint                 openssl  pkix-path before  after
  bar.example.com    none         excluded DNS:bar.example.com   Fail     Pass              Fail
  John Smith         email only   permitted DNS:example.com      OK       Pass              Pass
  notallowed.test    email only   permitted DNS:example.com      Fail     Pass              Fail

On the decision this bead asked for -- what counts as host-name shaped -- the rule is at least one label separator plus every label non-empty and LDH. That classifies both demonstrated cases the way OpenSSL does and keeps descriptive CNs out of the check entirely, which is where the false-rejection tail lives.

The coupling requirement from PKIX-bhtl applies again and caught something: a wildcard CN is NOT host-name shaped, yet pkix-identity's matcher honours wildcards, so checking only host-name-shaped CNs would have left the wildcard-CN hole open -- the very variant this investigation started from. is_dns_identity_shaped sits on top of is_hostname_shaped to admit wildcard spellings, and the CN then runs through the same dNSName machinery as a SAN, including wildcard_san_reaches_excluded_dns, rather than a parallel check that could drift.

Coverage note. Fixing pkix-path moved the refusal earlier, which made ConstrainedPathWithoutDnsId unreachable from both of PKIX-skxt's tests -- they stop at path validation now. That would have been a silent coverage regression in a security backstop. Added a third fixture, leaf-cn-in-subtree.der, whose CN is mx.good.example and therefore inside the permitted subtree: the path validates cleanly and the composition refusal is still the only thing refusing it. New test: the_composition_refusal_fires_when_the_path_itself_is_valid.

pkix-path 0.4.8 -> 0.4.9. INTEROP §9 updated with the fix and the not-a-live-bypass correction. AGENTS.md records the two lessons."}

{"notes":"SECOND CORRECTION, and the one that matters: the first version of this fix was over-strict and broke 88 x509-limbo testcases.

It matched OpenSSL, which bounds the commonName whenever no dNSName SAN is present. That rejects a certificate presenting IP:127.0.0.1 with CN=test.localhost under an excluded DNS:localhost -- bettertls::nameconstraints::tc5194 and 87 siblings, all expecting SUCCESS. The corpus went 49 ground-truth disagreements -> 137.

The certificate is asserting the address, not the name. RFC 5280 §4.1.2.6 makes subjectAltName the place identities live once it is present, so the CN is not an identity and bounding it refuses a certificate nobody can misuse. On that chain OpenSSL and pkix-path now both say Fail while limbo says SUCCESS -- limbo is right and OpenSSL is over-strict.

Condition narrowed to: no subjectAltName extension at all. Corpus back to 49, none regressed, family breakdown identical to baseline. The originally demonstrated hole (no SAN, CN=bar.example.com, excluded DNS:bar.example.com) is still closed. Row three of the INTEROP table -- host-name CN plus an email SAN -- is now a deliberate divergence from OpenSSL.

Root cause of my error: I used OpenSSL as the oracle and three hand-built chains as the evidence. All three agreed with the wrong rule. The corpus was already pinned and wired up and found it in one run. An implementation is evidence about a rule, not the rule.

Residual gap, documented rather than closed here: pkix-identity's CN fallback triggers on the absence of a dNSName SAN rather than of every SAN, so a certificate with an IP SAN and a host-name CN can still be CN-matched for a DNS name while unbounded by path validation. pkix-chain's ConstrainedPathWithoutDnsId refuses that shape unconditionally (PKIX-skxt), which is the right layer -- only it holds both the path and the requested name. If that coupling is ever wanted tighter, the lever is pkix-identity's fallback condition, not the constraint check.

Final state: 2822 workspace tests pass, limbo 49 disagreements (baseline), PKITS 246/249, clippy clean. pkix-path 0.4.9, committed, unpublished."}

Fixed in 10301abc, narrowly. See the notes for the two corrections this bead needed: it was not a live bypass (pkix-chain already refused the shape under PKIX-skxt), and the first fix was over-strict by copying OpenSSL, which cost 88 limbo testcases before being narrowed to 'no subjectAltName at all'.
